title: This day in history: Family accused of manslaughter was on trial is exorcism trial in Yakima. Heavyweight champion visited Spokane.
excerpt: From 1976: The defense rested in a bizarre exorcism/manslaughter trial in Yakima.
content:
From 1976: The defense rested in a bizarre exorcism/manslaughter trial in Yakima.

Five members of a religious household were charged with manslaughter after a 3-year-old boy died from a series of beatings “in an apparent crude form of exorcism, the Associated Press reported in an article that ran in The Spokesman-Review.

The 20-year-old mother of the boy, Debra Marie Wellbacher, “testified that she tried to love her son, but the child, possessed by a demonic spirit, rejected the love and said he hated her.”

One member of the household testified that the spankings administered to the young boy were “no big deal.”

“It wasn’t a ritual,” said the 27-year-old daughter of Leon Cunningham, the self-proclaimed minister of the group. “David (the boy) was not the center of attraction in the household – it was just an everyday thing.”

The defendants said “they left the body in a sealed room for several months in the belief that he would be resurrected.”

From 1926: “Gentleman Jim” Corbett, former heavyweight champion of the world, arrived mostly unheralded at the Davenport Hotel.

But the hotel’s page boys recognized him immediately, giving him a cheery, “Good mooning, Jim!”

A Spokane Chronicle reporter tracked him down at the hotel and wrote that he “holds his physique as trim as the day 34 years ago when he was acclaimed the new champion.”

“Just here for a 10-day visit,” said Gentleman Jim. “I open Sunday for a week at the Pantages with my partner, Bobby Barry, one of the best comedians on the stage today, I maintain.”

How did he stay in fighting trim at age 60?

“Diet and exercise,” he said. “I eat meat only once a day and beef only once in two weeks. I never drink ice water – it’s too cold for the stomach. I eat no white bread. and above all, I never worry. … I never drink liquor and I restrict my smoking to five cigars a day.”

In other news, the city of Spokane condemned a home at 606 W. Spofford perched on top of a large rock across from North Central High School. A hundred years later, the property remains vacant.

The newspaper referred it as a landmark sometimes known as the “S.L. Americus castle.” Americus, a former Hillyard attorney, had owned the home at one time, but the structure had been vacant for 18 years.
